The red circle on Bangladesh's flag is not in the middle.
It sits a little towards the pole, so that when the flag flies and flutters, the circle looks centred to people watching.
The first flag of Bangladesh had a yellow map of the country inside the red circle.
The map was dropped in 1972. One reason: it was hard to sew or paint correctly so it looked right from both sides.
Bangladesh and India once swapped 162 tiny pieces of land.
In 2015, 111 Indian enclaves inside Bangladesh and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves inside India changed hands, and about 50,000 people chose their country.
Before 2015, a field near Kurigram was the world's only 'enclave inside an enclave inside an enclave'.
Dahala Khagrabari was a bit of India, inside a bit of Bangladesh, inside a bit of India, inside Bangladesh. The 2015 land swap ended it.
Bhutan was the first country to recognise Bangladesh, on 6 December 1971.
India followed a few hours later the same day, ten days before the war ended.
Bangladesh only joined the United Nations in 1974.
China blocked its entry with a veto in 1972. Bangladesh finally became a member on 17 September 1974.
About 93,000 soldiers surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December 1971.
It was one of the largest surrenders since the Second World War, signed at the Ramna Race Course, now Suhrawardy Udyan.
The very first Shaheed Minar was built overnight by students in February 1952.
They put it up on 23 February to honour those killed on 21 February. Police knocked it down a few days later, and the monument we know came later.
Dhaka was given a royal name in 1610: Jahangirnagar.
Mughal governor Islam Khan made Dhaka the capital of Bengal and named it after Emperor Jahangir.
Lalbagh Fort in Old Dhaka was never finished.
Work stopped after Pari Bibi, the daughter of governor Shaista Khan, died there in 1684. Her tomb still stands inside the fort.
Ahsan Manzil, the pink palace by the Buriganga, is where many say Dhaka first saw electric light.
The Nawabs of Dhaka lived there, and their palace was lit with electricity in 1901, long before most homes in the city.
The Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat does not have sixty domes.
Its main hall has 77 small domes, held up by about 60 stone pillars. It was built in the 1400s by Khan Jahan Ali.
Paharpur in Naogaon was one of the biggest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas.
Somapura Mahavihara was built around the 700s by the Pala king Dharmapala and had about 177 small rooms for monks around a huge temple.
Wari-Bateshwar in Narsingdi was a walled town around 2,500 years ago.
Archaeologists found old coins, glass beads and a brick road there, showing it traded with faraway places.
Mahasthangarh in Bogura is one of the oldest city sites in Bangladesh.
A stone found there carries writing in Brahmi script from around the 3rd century BCE.
The Kantajew Temple in Dinajpur tells whole stories in clay.
Its walls are covered with thousands of terracotta tiles showing scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and daily life in the 1700s.
Cox's Bazar is named after a British officer, Captain Hiram Cox.
He was sent there in the 1790s to help settle refugees from Arakan, and died in 1799 before finishing the job.
Saint Martin's Island is Bangladesh's only coral island.
Local people call it Narikel Jinjira, which means coconut island.
Bhola is the largest island in Bangladesh.
It sits where the Meghna meets the Bay of Bengal and is home to around two million people.
Bangladesh's highest peak is still argued over.
Tajingdong was long listed as the highest, but surveys suggest Saka Haphong in Bandarban, about 1,050 metres tall, is higher.
Kaptai Lake in Rangamati is man-made.
It formed when the Kaptai Dam blocked the Karnaphuli River in 1962. The water covered farms, villages and the old Chakma royal palace.
A deep underwater canyon lies off the coast of Bangladesh.
The Swatch of No Ground drops more than 1,000 metres. Dolphins, whales and sharks live there, and it became a marine protected area in 2014.
Bangladesh won a huge area of sea in two court cases.
Rulings against Myanmar in 2012 and India in 2014 settled its sea borders, giving it more than 118,000 square kilometres of water.
The Ganges river dolphin in Bangladesh's rivers is almost blind.
It finds fish by sending out clicks and listening for the echo, a skill called echolocation.
The western hoolock gibbon in Lawachara forest is Bangladesh's only ape.
Hoolock gibbons are the only apes in South Asia. Families call to each other with loud songs at dawn.
A 2018 count found 114 tigers in the Bangladesh part of the Sundarbans.
Sundarbans tigers are strong swimmers and cross wide river channels between islands.
The Sundarbans is probably named after one tree.
The sundari tree grows all over the forest. Most of the mangrove forest is in Bangladesh, the rest in India.
Ratargul in Sylhet is a forest that stands in water for months.
It is a freshwater swamp forest. In the rainy season the trees stand in several metres of water and people move through it by boat.
Tanguar Haor was Bangladesh's second Ramsar wetland of world importance.
It was listed in 2000, after the Sundarbans in 1992. Winter brings huge flocks of migrating ducks and other birds.
Farmers in Gopalganj and Barishal grow vegetables on floating rafts.
The rafts are made from water hyacinth. In 2015, the UN's food agency listed this as a farming system of world importance.
Bangladesh produces most of the world's hilsa fish.
Hilsa swim up from the sea into rivers to lay eggs, so catching them is banned for about three weeks in October to protect them.
Jamdani was Bangladesh's first product with a Geographical Indication label.
It got the label in 2016, and hilsa followed in 2017. The label says a product comes from a certain place and is made in its traditional way.
UNESCO listed Jamdani weaving as world heritage in 2013.
Weavers add the patterns thread by thread on the loom, so one fine sari can take months.
Dhaka's rickshaw art is on UNESCO's heritage list.
It was added in 2023. Painters decorate rickshaws with film stars, birds, flowers and buildings in bright colours.
Sylhet's cool mat, shital pati, is world heritage too.
Weavers split a green cane called murta into thin strips. UNESCO listed the craft in 2017.
Baul songs from Bangladesh were among the first things UNESCO named as world heritage of this kind.
Bauls are wandering singers. Lalon Shah is the best known, and his songs are still sung everywhere.
Dhaka muslin was once so fine that a long piece could pass through a ring.
It was made from a cotton called phuti karpas that grew along the Meghna. Scientists have been trying to bring the plant and the cloth back.
The first commercial tea garden in Bangladesh opened in Sylhet in 1854.
It is called Malnicherra. Today Bangladesh has more than 160 tea gardens.
Scientists in Bangladesh decoded the jute plant's genes.
A team led by Maqsudul Alam announced it in 2010. Knowing the genes helps breed better jute, the golden fibre.
The Parliament building in Dhaka was designed by an American architect who never saw it finished.
Louis Kahn died in 1974. The building was completed in 1982 and is famous for its huge geometric openings.
The Padma Bridge stands on some of the deepest bridge piles in the world.
Some steel piles go about 120 metres into the riverbed, because the Padma's bottom is soft and moves.
Bangladesh paid for the Padma Bridge with its own money.
The World Bank pulled out of the loan in 2012. The 6.15 km bridge opened in June 2022.
Bangladesh's first satellite flew on a new kind of rocket's first ever flight.
In May 2018 it launched on SpaceX's first Falcon 9 Block 5, the rocket version that later flew dozens of times.
The Hardinge Bridge over the Padma is more than 100 years old.
It opened in 1915 near Paksey. It was damaged in 1971 and repaired, and trains still cross it.
A tiny spelling mistake stopped part of the biggest bank robbery attempt in Bangladesh.
In 2016, hackers tried to move about 951 million dollars from Bangladesh Bank. A misspelled word in one order made a bank stop and check.
Old Dhaka has an Armenian church from 1781.
Armenian traders once lived in Armanitola. The Church of the Holy Resurrection still stands there.
Panam Nagar in Sonargaon is a whole street of empty old houses.
Rich cloth merchants built them about 150 years ago. Sonargaon itself was once a capital of Bengal.
Bakarkhani, the flaky bread of Old Dhaka, comes with a love story.
Legend says it is named after Aga Baqir and a dancer called Khani Begum. It has been sold in Old Dhaka for centuries.
Dhaka University, founded in 1921, was nicknamed 'the Oxford of the East'.
Students from there led many big moments, including the 1952 Language Movement.
Bangladesh counts six seasons, not four.
Grishma, Barsha, Sharat, Hemanta, Sheet and Basanta. Each lasts about two months of the Bangla calendar.
The Bangla calendar is linked to farm taxes.
It is traditionally said to have started under Mughal emperor Akbar so taxes could be collected after the harvest. Pohela Boishakh is its New Year.
Bangla is one of the most spoken languages in the world.
More than 230 million people speak it as a first language, in Bangladesh, India and around the world.
The Concert for Bangladesh in 1971 was the first big charity rock concert.
George Harrison and Ravi Shankar held it in New York to raise money for refugees. Later shows like Live Aid copied the idea.
Bangladesh has tens of thousands of trained cyclone volunteers.
The Cyclone Preparedness Programme started in 1972. Volunteers go door to door with warnings, which has saved huge numbers of lives.
The Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna carry about a billion tonnes of mud to the sea each year.
That sediment built the Bengal delta, the largest river delta in the world, on which most of Bangladesh sits.
Jackfruit, the national fruit, is the biggest fruit that grows on a tree.
One jackfruit can weigh more than 30 kilograms and grows straight out of the trunk.
Teknaf to Cox's Bazar has one of the longest sea-side roads in the country.
The Marine Drive runs about 80 kilometres with hills on one side and the beach on the other.
The Chittagong Hill Tracts are home to more than ten different peoples.
They include the Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Mro and Bawm, each with their own language and festivals.
Kazi Nazrul Islam wrote and tuned thousands of songs.
Nazrul Geeti cover love, rebellion, nature and devotion. He was brought to Dhaka in 1972 and named the national poet.
The four names on the 1952 Language Movement memorial are known across the country.
Salam, Barkat, Rafiq and Jabbar were among those killed on 21 February 1952 while demanding Bangla as a state language.
Avro Keyboard, free Bangla typing software, was made by a Bangladeshi doctor.
Mehdi Hasan Khan released it in 2003, and it helped millions of people type Bangla on computers.
